chunks.title: Who Vineeth is
chunks.text: Vineeth Reddy Kodakandla is an ML engineer based in New Jersey who works on model inference and evaluation: how fast and how cheaply models run on real hardware, and whether their output holds up. He completed an M.S. in Computer Science at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi (August 2024 to May 2026). Before that he worked on LLM serving at EXL (Noida, India, September 2023 to August 2024) and on real-time vision inference at L&T Technology Services (Bengaluru, India, January 2022 to July 2023). His public projects are measurement studies: bitwise-forensics, which measures whether a continuous-batching engine returns the same greedy tokens when requests are batched together; the Meteor Lake Latency Lab, which measures which processor on an Intel laptop chip should run live instance segmentation; and the LLM Eval Observatory, a nightly evaluation of open-weight models on anti-money-laundering alert triage. Every measured result on his site links to the committed file it came from.

chunks.title: Roles he is looking for
chunks.text: Vineeth is looking for ML engineer, inference engineer and software engineering roles, especially work on model serving, performance and evaluation. He is based in New Jersey and open to relocation and to remote roles. The best way to start a conversation is email at vineethkodakandla@gmail.com.

chunks.title: Project: bitwise-forensics (token changes under continuous batching)
chunks.text:
bitwise-forensics is Vineeth's LLM-serving measurement project (public repository github.com/vineethkodakandla/bitwise-forensics, version 0.3.0; case study on this site at /work/bitwise-forensics). It asks whether a serving engine returns the same greedy tokens for a prompt when other requests share its engine steps. He measured OpenVINO GenAI 2026.3's ContinuousBatchingPipeline serving Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B-Instruct with INT4 weights, greedy decoding and up to 128 new tokens, on the Arc iGPU and the CPU of an Intel Core Ultra 7 155H. The prompts are 40 short instructions built from 4 templates and 10 LLM-serving topics. Each prompt is served alone for a batch-of-1 reference, then all 40 arrive on Poisson schedules and share engine steps. Load is an arrival rate from c2 to c32, meaning arrivals per maximum-length generation on a virtual clock of 20 ms engine steps; it is not a number of users. Each configuration ran 8 trials, so each row covers 320 runs and the study has 7,680 runs.

Under default settings, a batched run's tokens differed from the same prompt's batch-of-1 output in 95.6 to 100 percent of iGPU runs and 54.4 to 72.5 percent of CPU runs. The two devices run different quantized defaults (iGPU: f16 activations, 4-bit KV cache, dynamic quantization group size 32; CPU: f32 activations, 8-bit KV cache, dynamic quantization group size 32), so the difference between them is not a hardware comparison. On the CPU the share rose from c2 to c4 by 18.1 points (95% CI 5.3 to 30.3), and no change was detected at higher rates.

Replaying the eight c8 arrival schedules with default options, in the same process, reproduced all 320 runs on each device bit for bit (tokens, chosen-token logprobs and per-step batch sizes), and batch-of-1 output was bitwise identical across repeated passes for every option set. So where tested, the output was a fixed function of the arrival schedule, and a different schedule could change it.

On the CPU at c8, turning off dynamic activation quantization cut the share of runs with changed tokens from 71.2 to 21.2 percent (paired 95% CI for the drop: 34.7 to 64.4 points). An f32 KV cache alone did not change the share (+0.3 points, 95% CI -14.7 to +15.0). With both settings, 0 of 320 runs had changed tokens at c8 and 0 of 320 at c32; the exact 95% upper bound is 1.1 percent counting runs and 8.8 percent counting prompts. That setting is not batch-invariant, because chosen-token logprobs still differed from batch-of-1 in every one of those runs, by at most 2.9e-5. On the iGPU no tested setting removed the changes: an f16 KV cache lowered the c8 share to 51.2 percent, turning off dynamic quantization left it at 100 percent, and float32 settings did not run. Splitting prompt processing into 16-token steps raised the CPU c8 share from 71.2 to 90.0 percent.

Method: per-row bootstrap intervals over prompts and trials widened to exact Clopper-Pearson intervals, paired comparisons on identical arrival schedules, a replay control, batch-of-1 checks before and after the trials, committed per-token results with the scripts that rebuild every README number, and 175 tests in CI on Linux and Windows. The project began as a simulator; across 12 synthetic-model seeds its load trend changed direction, so the simulator is kept only as a pipeline test. Stated limits: one engine, one small model, one laptop, greedy decoding, 40 short templated prompts, no measurement of output quality (so nothing about batched outputs being better or worse), no attribution to a specific operation, no comparison with other engines, and intervals not adjusted for multiple comparisons.

chunks.title: Project: Meteor Lake Latency Lab (edge inference latency)
chunks.text:
The Meteor Lake Latency Lab is Vineeth's edge-inference project (public repository github.com/vineethkodakandla/edge-vision-lab; case study on this site at /work/meteor-lake-latency-lab). It asks which processor on one laptop chip, an Intel Core Ultra 7 155H, should run live instance segmentation within a 33.3 ms per-frame budget: the NPU, the Arc integrated GPU or the CPU. The model is YOLOv8n-seg at a fixed 640 by 640 input through OpenVINO 2026.3, in FP32, FP16 and two INT8 builds made with NNCF post-training quantization on 300 COCO val2017 images. One INT8 build keeps the detection-head decode in float and the other quantizes everything. Accuracy is measured on the other 4,700 images. The benchmark discards 100 warm-up frames and times 1,000 frames per configuration with 45 s cooldowns, covering preprocess, inference and NumPy postprocess.

In the flat-out benchmark, INT8 on the iGPU had an 11.3 ms median but a 47.0 ms p99, while INT8 on the NPU had a 13.9 ms median and an 18.0 ms p99. On a live webcam loop (one 60 s session each, 2,398 iGPU frames and 1,891 NPU frames) the iGPU ran a 10.4 ms median and 13.3 ms p99, ahead of the NPU at 18.0 ms and 22.3 ms, although it missed the budget on 0.33 percent of frames against the NPU's 0.05 percent. So the ranking depends on how busy the accelerator is kept. The iGPU's flat-out tail came from CPU-side stalls, defined as frames where preprocess plus postprocess took more than 20 ms: the iGPU produced 63 stall frames in 4,000 against 6 for the NPU and 1 for the CPU, and without stall frames the iGPU INT8 p99 is 17.1 ms while its inference-only p99 was 9.5 ms. The cause of the stalls is not attributed; separating display compositor contention, the shared package power budget and driver threads would need ETW tracing.

Keeping the detection-head decode in float cost 0.0015 box mAP on the CPU; quantizing everything cost 0.0389, about 26 times as much, for a 0.35 ms faster NPU median. INT8 cost 0.0024 box mAP on the iGPU and 0.0023 on the NPU against the CPU FP32 reference. Stated limits: power was not measured; one model and input size on one machine; only the two INT8 configurations were run live, for one session each; and the live loop does not wait for new camera frames, so it ran busier than a strict 30 fps camera.

chunks.title: Project: LLM Eval Observatory (nightly LLM evaluation)
chunks.text:
The LLM Eval Observatory is Vineeth's evaluation project (public repository github.com/vineethkodakandla/llm-eval-observatory, dashboard llm-eval-observatory.vercel.app; case study on this site at /work/llm-eval-observatory). A GitHub Action runs nightly against open-weight models on Groq's free tier and commits latest.json and history.jsonl back to the repository, and a Next.js dashboard on Vercel reads them. The main track asks whether a model can triage anti-money-laundering alerts: 26 hand-written synthetic cases (14 escalate, 8 clear, 4 review), each answered as ESCALATE, CLEAR or REVIEW with cited evidence, and scored by a deterministic parser rather than by another model. It reports decision accuracy, typology accuracy, citation faithfulness, fabricated-citation rate, false-clear rate (clearing a case that should have been escalated, the dangerous miss) and whether ambiguous cases are sent to review. The other tracks are a 30-prompt injection and jailbreak battery in which quoting the payload counts as a breach, a 50-item capability set with drift detection, and an LLM-as-judge reliability check on 24 human-labelled pairwise items using Cohen's and Fleiss' kappa. Intervals are percentile bootstraps with 5,000 seeded resamples; drift is flagged only when a score moves at least 5 points and the intervals do not overlap; a night where every model is skipped does not overwrite earlier results.

From 2 August to 15 September 2026, GPT-OSS 120B completed the triage track on 29 nights and never cleared a case that should have been escalated, with accuracy between 92.3 and 100 percent on the same cases. It defended 93.3 to 96.7 percent of injection attacks over 31 nights, and Llama 3.3 70B defended 73.3 to 83.3 percent over the 19 nights it completed. Models are skipped on nights when they are unavailable or rate-limited, and on recent nights 2 of the 5 configured models have finished; the case study page shows the latest run live. Stated limits: the cases are synthetic and self-authored, so this is not a compliance benchmark; samples are small (4 ambiguous cases, so review routing moves in 25-point steps); several scores sit at the ceiling; the judges come from one vendor; and drift is compared only with the previous night.

chunks.title: Project: Edith (multi-agent pipeline with a release gate)
chunks.text: Edith is a browser demo of a multi-agent pipeline (live at vineethkodakandla.github.io/edith-lab, source github.com/vineethkodakandla/edith-lab). Researcher, Analyst, Critic and Synthesizer agents run in a fixed order over a shared blackboard. The Critic can send a draft back once, and a rule-based Governor withholds any recommendation that has no retrieved source behind it and marks it for human review. By default it is deterministic, retrieving by term-frequency cosine similarity over an 8-document built-in corpus; with a visitor's own Groq key the four agents make real Llama 3.1 8B and Llama 3.3 70B calls, while the Governor stays rule-based. It is written as framework-free JavaScript modules with no build step. It is a small demo of orchestration and a release gate, not a production system, and its keyword-based retrieval can match off-topic questions.

chunks.title: Project: ANANTA (agent memory that forgets)
chunks.text: ANANTA is a browser demo of agent memory that forgets on purpose (live at vineethkodakandla.github.io/ananta-lab, source github.com/vineethkodakandla/ananta-lab). Each memory decays on an Ebbinghaus forgetting curve, each recall raises the memory's stability, a manual decay pass prunes memories whose retention has fallen below 2 percent, and every write is chained with SHA-256 through Web Crypto, so editing a stored memory makes verification fail. A deterministic agent loop sits on top: lexical retrieval over 8 built-in documents, keyword-scored difficulty bands that pick a model tier, and abstaining when retrieval is thin. With a visitor's own Groq key the draft step becomes a real model call. It is a small, inspectable demo rather than a production memory system.

chunks.title: This site and its assistant
chunks.text: This portfolio site is a Next.js application deployed on Vercel (source github.com/vineethkodakandla/vineeth-portfolio). Its assistant uses retrieval-augmented generation: each question is embedded with Voyage, the closest passages are found by cosine search with pgvector in a Neon Postgres database, and Claude writes the answer from those passages, which are listed under the answer. The case-study charts are built from the projects' committed result files, and the LLM Eval Observatory panel reads that project's latest results file and refreshes at most hourly.

chunks.title: Experience: EXL (2023 to 2024)
chunks.text: From September 2023 to August 2024 Vineeth worked at EXL in Noida, India, on LLM serving for insurance underwriting and claims work. He worked on the Amazon Bedrock serving path (prompt routing, context-window management and token streaming), on evaluation runs that compared fine-tuned models with commercial models, and on the latency and cost dashboards the team used. He contributed pre-launch engineering to LDS Underwriting Assist, which EXL launched in August 2024. Outcomes EXL has published for that product are company results, not his personal metrics. Figures from his own work there are internal and are not published on this site; for more detail, contact him directly.

chunks.title: Experience: L&T Technology Services (2022 to 2023)
chunks.text: From January 2022 to July 2023 Vineeth worked at L&T Technology Services in Bengaluru, India, where he started as an intern, on real-time inference for endoscopy video, covering image enhancement and polyp detection, using NVIDIA's Holoscan SDK and developer kits. He moved models from PyTorch to ONNX Runtime and TensorRT with FP16 and INT8 quantization checked against FP32, restructured the input pipeline to reduce per-frame latency, and wrote the benchmarking scripts used to compare edge targets. Figures from that work are internal and are not published on this site; for more detail, contact him directly.

chunks.title: Education and certification
chunks.text: Vineeth earned an M.S. in Computer Science at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi (August 2024 to May 2026). He was a graduate research assistant under Dr. Carlos Rubio-Medrano, working on rule-based multi-agent access control with ABAC and XACML, and a teaching assistant for Computer Forensics. His coursework included computer architecture, advanced software engineering, network security and agent-based systems. He holds Anthropic's Building with the Claude API certification.

chunks.title: Tools and methods
chunks.text: Inference and optimization: OpenVINO and OpenVINO GenAI, NNCF post-training quantization, ONNX Runtime and TensorRT, FP16 and INT8 quantization, continuous batching. Measurement: latency distributions and frame budgets, bootstrap confidence intervals, paired comparisons, replay and reproducibility checks, benchmark automation. LLM applications and evaluation: evaluation harnesses, prompt-injection testing, LLM-as-judge reliability, retrieval-augmented generation, Amazon Bedrock. Engineering: Python, TypeScript, C++, SQL, NumPy, pandas, PyTorch, FastAPI, React, Next.js, PostgreSQL with pgvector, Docker, Kubernetes and GitHub Actions. The public projects show the inference, measurement and evaluation work end to end.

chunks.title: How he approaches problems
chunks.text: Vineeth's projects usually start from a claim that is easy to repeat and then check where it holds: that a benchmark picks the right processor for a camera, that greedy decoding gives the same tokens when requests are batched together, that a model can triage alerts without a person reading each one. The answer is usually that it depends, and the useful part is finding out on what. He publishes what a result does not show alongside what it does, and drops results that fail a check: bitwise-forensics began as a simulator and moved to a real engine after a check across 12 seeds showed that the simulated load trend was not stable.
